name: Longest Same-Category Shelf Run
description:
An Amazon fulfilment centre has n items on one long shelf, left to right. Each item has a category, written as an uppercase letter, in the string s. To make picking faster, the team wants a run of consecutive items that all have the same category. Before choosing the run, they may relabel at most k items (a relabelled item gets any category they like).

Some items are locked (lock[i] = '1'): their category is printed on the box and can never be relabelled. Unlocked items have lock[i] = '0'.

Find the length of the longest run of consecutive items that can be made all the same category.

Example: s = AABABBA, lock = 0000000, k = 1. Items 1 to 4 are A A B A: relabel the B and they become AAAA, a run of 4. No run of 5 can be made with one relabel, so the answer is 4.

Previously asked: Amazon SDE online assessment, September 2025 (longest window with at most k changes). This version adds locked items.

Input: The first line has n and k. The second line has the string s. The third line has the string lock (both of length n).
Output: One integer, the length of the longest run.

Constraints:
- 1 <= n <= 20000
- 0 <= k <= n
- s has only uppercase letters A to Z
- lock has only the characters 0 and 1

test_cases.description: Items 1 to 4 are A A B A: relabel the B to get 4 A's in a row. No run of 5 needs only one change.
Item 3 (B) is locked, so a run of A's cannot include it. Items 3 to 6 are B A B B: relabel the A to get 4 B's, and the locked B is already B.

name: Peak Load on the Delivery Road
description:
n Amazon delivery vans use the same narrow road. Van i is on the road from minute start[i] up to, but not including, minute end[i], and it weighs w[i] tonnes. So a van that leaves at minute 10 and another that arrives at minute 10 are never on the road together.

The road authority needs the largest total weight that is ever on the road at the same time, and the earliest minute at which that weight is first reached.

Example: vans (1, 5, 4), (2, 6, 3), (5, 8, 6). From minute 2 to 5 the first two vans give 7 tonnes. At minute 5 the first van leaves and the third arrives: 3 + 6 = 9 tonnes. The answer is 9 tonnes, first reached at minute 5.

Pattern reported in 2026 Amazon online assessments: overlapping delivery windows (sorting + sweep line).

Input: The first line has n. Each of the next n lines has start[i], end[i] and w[i].
Output: Two integers separated by a space: the largest total weight, and the earliest minute it is reached.

Constraints:
- 1 <= n <= 20000
- 0 <= start[i] < end[i] <= 1000000000
- 1 <= w[i] <= 10000

solution.code:
import sys, heapq
from collections import deque, defaultdict

def peak_load(vans):
    events = []
    for s, e, w in vans:
        events.append((s, 1, w))
        events.append((e, 0, -w))
    events.sort()
    cur = best = 0
    best_t = None
    for t, kind, w in events:
        cur += w
        if kind == 1 and cur > best:
            best, best_t = cur, t
    return f"{best} {best_t}"

t = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
if t:
    n = t[0]
    print(peak_load([tuple(t[1 + 3 * i:4 + 3 * i]) for i in range(n)]))

test_cases.description: At minute 5 van 1 has left and van 3 has arrived: 3 + 6 = 9 tonnes, more than the 7 tonnes from minute 2 to 5.
The first two vans never overlap (the road is free of van 1 at minute 10). The peak is 5 + 1 = 6 at minute 3.

name: Build Order for One Package
description:
Amazon's build system has n software packages, numbered 1 to n. A dependency pair "a b" means package a needs package b, so b must be built before a.

An engineer wants to build only one package, target, together with every package it needs directly or indirectly. Other packages must not be built. When several needed packages are ready (all their own needs are already built), the build system always builds the one with the smallest number first.

Print the build order. If the needed packages contain a circular dependency, nothing can be built: print -1.

Example: n = 5, pairs (4 needs 2), (4 needs 3), (3 needs 1), (5 needs 1), target 4. Needed packages: 4, 2, 3, 1 (package 5 is not needed). Ready at the start: 1 and 2, so build 1, then 2. Now 3 is ready, then 4. The order is 1 2 3 4.

Previously asked: Amazon Software Engineer technical screen, July 2026 (full build order for one target package; Course Schedule II with a twist).

Input: The first line has n, m (number of pairs) and target. Each of the next m lines has a pair a b.
Output: The build order as numbers separated by spaces, or -1.

Constraints:
- 1 <= n <= 20000
- 0 <= m <= 50000
- 1 <= a, b, target <= n, a != b, no pair is repeated

test_cases.description: Needed: 1, 2, 3, 4. Build 1 and 2 first (smallest ready first), then 3, then the target 4. Package 5 is not needed.
Package 1 needs 2, and 2, 3, 4 need each other in a circle, so nothing can be built: -1.

name: Earliest Finish for the Launch Plan
description:
A product launch has n jobs, numbered 1 to n. Job i takes dur[i] days and cannot start before day rel[i] (for example, a vendor delivers its inputs on that day). A pair "a b" means job a can start only after job b has finished. There are as many workers as needed, so any number of jobs can run on the same day.

Each job starts as early as possible: on the later of rel[i] and the finish day of its last required job. It finishes dur[i] days after it starts. Print the day on which the last job finishes. If the requirements contain a circle, the launch can never finish: print -1.

Example: dur = [3, 2, 4], rel = [0, 5, 0], pairs (3 after 1), (3 after 2). Job 1 runs days 0 to 3. Job 2 cannot start before day 5, so it runs 5 to 7. Job 3 waits for both: it starts on day 7 and finishes on day 11. The answer is 11.

Pattern: Amazon course-order and dependency questions, 2026 (topological sort), with a longest-path DP over the order.

Input: The first line has n and m. The second line has dur[1..n]. The third line has rel[1..n]. Each of the next m lines has a pair a b.
Output: One integer, the finish day of the last job, or -1.

Constraints:
- 1 <= n <= 20000
- 0 <= m <= 50000
- 1 <= dur[i] <= 10000
- 0 <= rel[i] <= 100000000
- a != b, no pair is repeated

solution.code:
import sys, heapq
from collections import deque, defaultdict

def earliest_finish(n, dur, rel, deps):
    preds = defaultdict(list)
    users = defaultdict(list)
    indeg = [0] * (n + 1)
    for a, b in deps:
        preds[a].append(b)
        users[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(1, n + 1) if indeg[i] == 0)
    finish = [0] * (n + 1)
    done = 0
    while q:
        x = q.popleft()
        done += 1
        start = max([rel[x - 1]] + [finish[p] for p in preds[x]])
        finish[x] = start + dur[x - 1]
        for u in users[x]:
            indeg[u] -= 1
            if indeg[u] == 0:
                q.append(u)
    if done < n:
        return -1
    return max(finish[1:])

x = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
if x:
    n, m = x[0], x[1]
    dur, rel, o = x[2:2 + n], x[2 + n:2 + 2 * n], 2 + 2 * n
    print(earliest_finish(n, dur, rel, [(x[o + 2 * i], x[o + 1 + 2 * i]) for i in range(m)]))

name: Minimum Starting Charge for the Drone
description:
A delivery drone flies over a warehouse floor of R rows and C columns, from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. Each cell has a number: a negative number is the battery it uses to cross that cell, a positive number is a charging pad that adds battery, and 0 changes nothing. The cell's number applies as soon as the drone enters it, including the first and the last cell.

The battery must stay at 1 or more at every moment, or the drone falls. Find the smallest whole starting battery that lets the drone reach the bottom-right cell along some path.

Example: grid = [[-2, -3, 3], [-5, -10, 1], [10, 30, -5]]. Going right, right, down, down uses 2 and 3, charges 3 and 1, then uses 5: starting with 7 the battery goes 5, 2, 5, 6, 1. With 6 it would reach 0 at the end. The answer is 7.

Pattern: grid path DP reported in Amazon SDE-1 interviews (Grid Maximum Sum Path, January 2025). This version must be filled from the bottom-right corner.

Input: The first line has R and C. Each of the next R lines has C integers.
Output: One integer, the smallest starting battery.

Constraints:
- 1 <= R, C <= 200
- -1000 <= each cell <= 1000

solution.code:
import sys, heapq
from collections import deque, defaultdict

def min_battery(g):
    R, C = len(g), len(g[0])
    INF = float('inf')
    need = [[INF] * (C + 1) for _ in range(R + 1)]
    need[R][C - 1] = need[R - 1][C] = 1
    for r in range(R - 1, -1, -1):
        for c in range(C - 1, -1, -1):
            need[r][c] = max(1, min(need[r + 1][c], need[r][c + 1]) - g[r][c])
    return need[0][0]

x = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
if x:
    r, c = x[0], x[1]
    print(min_battery([x[2 + i * c:2 + (i + 1) * c] for i in range(r)]))

test_cases.description: Right, right, down, down: starting with 7 the battery goes 5, 2, 5, 6, 1 and never drops below 1. With 6 it would hit 0 on the last cell.
Right then down: starting with 4 the battery goes 4, 9, 1. Down then right would need 13. The answer is 4.

name: Cheapest Label Correction
description:
A warehouse scanner read a shipping label as the string a, but the correct label is b. A correction tool can change a, one letter at a time, using three operations:
- insert one letter anywhere, cost ins;
- delete one letter, cost del;
- replace one letter with a different letter, cost rep.

Find the smallest total cost to turn a into exactly b. Note that replacing is not always the best choice: when rep is larger than ins + del, deleting and inserting is cheaper.

Example: a = kitten, b = sitting, ins = 1, del = 1, rep = 1. Replace k with s, replace e with i, and insert g at the end: cost 3. With rep = 5 instead, each replacement is cheaper as a delete plus an insert (cost 2), so the answer becomes 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.

Previously asked: Edit Distance, Amazon New Grad software engineer onsite, July 2026. This version has a different cost for each operation.

Input: The first line has ins, del and rep. The second line has a. The third line has b.
Output: One integer, the smallest total cost.

Constraints:
- 1 <= length of a, length of b <= 1000
- a and b have only lowercase letters
- 1 <= ins, del, rep <= 1000

test_cases.description: Replace k with s, replace e with i, insert g: 3 operations of cost 1.
Replacing costs 5, but delete + insert costs 2, so each of the two changed letters costs 2, plus 1 to insert g: 5.
